paras: The McNally stabbing in Baltimore took place on the evening of 21 June 1882, when boys threw stones at a parading Black division of the Grand Army of the Republic and a member of the column fatally stabbed Bernard McNally, a youth standing at the corner of Madison and Constitution streets. George H. Brightman, the Black vice-commander of Lincoln Post, was charged with murder after a coroner's jury named him, but he was acquitted in December 1882 when the state conceded its evidence was insufficient.

The clash came on the last day of the national encampment of the Grand Army of the Republic in Baltimore, as a section of the Black posts marched home from Schützen Park. Lincoln Post No. 7, whose officers included Brightman, was among the marching units.

At the corner of Madison and Constitution streets, boys of the neighborhood began throwing stones into the ranks of the veterans. According to the wire report, the attackers were 'a gang of juvenile rowdies' and 'the colored men charged on the rabble.' The column broke up, and witnesses said some marchers left the ranks while the commander tried in vain to restore order.

McNally was standing on the sidewalk beside his uncle's store when a Black officer with a drawn sabre struck at him twice, the Baltimore Deutsche Correspondent reported from the inquest testimony. The first blow knocked down a Black man standing nearby with the flat of the blade, and the second wounded McNally in the side as he raised his arm; the attacker then left with the other marchers. McNally, whom the Baltimore paper gave as 19 and the wire as 18, seemed to improve on Thursday but died on Friday evening, 23 June.

Police at first had no trace of the attacker, and they told the Deutsche Correspondent that McNally himself had been the leader of the boys throwing stones. Officers of Lincoln Post were summoned to the inquest on 24 June, where Brightman was identified as the man who struck the blow, though witnesses disagreed. The jury found that McNally died of a sabre wound inflicted by Brightman, a 34-year-old laborer, who was jailed to await the grand jury.

The grand jury presented Brightman for murder, with bail set at $5,000, and indicted him on 12 July. At his trial before Judge Phelps on 18 December, without a jury, the post-mortem physician said the sabre police had shown him could not have made the wound, and the eyewitness Michael Featherstone said the stabber was a head taller and much darker than Brightman. After a post officer testified that Brightman had stayed at the front keeping the ranks in order, State's Attorney Kerr said the state lacked sufficient evidence, and the judge acquitted Brightman of murder.

Outside Baltimore the episode ran as a one-sentence wire item in news-digest columns, first in the Bismarck Tribune on 23 June, which reported McNally killed on the spot. A shorter version, saying the boys' stoning 'was resented' and calling the victim 'Robt. McNally,' ran in late June and July in small papers in Tennessee, Arkansas, Mississippi and Louisiana. The New York Sun and the Lancaster Intelligencer carried the inquest under the headlines 'Fatally Stabbed by One of the Grand Army' and 'An Ex Soldier Held for Murder,' identifying Brightman as 'colored.' In Maryland, the Westminster Democratic Advocate noted in its state column that 'Brightman, the colored Grand Army officer' had been charged with the murder of 'young McNally.'

The fullest coverage came from Baltimore's German-language Deutsche Correspondent, which described the grief of McNally's family and neighborhood while also printing the police view that he had led the stone-throwers. That paper followed the case through the inquest, the indictment and the trial, reporting the witnesses' doubts about Brightman's guilt and his acquittal.

The wire called the victim Robert, while the Baltimore paper, the inquest dispatch and the court records named him Bernard. Reports also differed on the weapon, a knife thrust in the first German accounts and a sword or sabre in the inquest reports and verdict.

bases: Boys stoned a parading Black G.A.R. post (A1, A9, A17); the one death was of a youth stabbed by a Black marcher in response (A6).
The wire (A1, A9), the New York Sun (A3) and the Baltimore German paper (A2, A6, A17) independently agree on the stoning and the fatal stabbing; the attacker's identity was contested (A6, A17).

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A Black G.A.R. post was attacked by boys with stones; the veterans 'charged on the rabble' or 'resented' it, and McNally was killed or fatally cut.

accounts.label: Baltimore police
accounts.gist: Police said McNally himself was the guilty party and the leader of the boys who threw stones at the Black marchers.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: McNally died of a sabre wound and the sabre was in Brightman's hands.

accounts.label: Defense witnesses at trial
accounts.gist: An eyewitness said the stabber was a head taller and much darker than Brightman; a post officer said Brightman stayed at the front of the column.

framing.detail: Wire briefs ran the clash in news-digest columns, calling the attackers 'juvenile rowdies' and 'the rabble' and saying the attack 'was resented'.
The New York Sun headed its dispatch 'Fatally Stabbed by One of the Grand Army'; Lancaster used 'An Ex Soldier Held for Murder'.
The Baltimore German paper mourned McNally's death and called the boys 'etwas zu übermüthig', but reported the police view that he led the stone-throwers and covered witness doubts and the acquittal.
